strengths: The word/event analogy (index+position, finite dictionary, context-determined meaning) is a clean and pedagogically useful framing that connects event-based vision to NLP-style tokenization.

The parametric spatial embedding (Algorithm 1) is a simple mechanism to inject neighborhood inductive bias, and the Taylor-series argument for why nearby coordinates receive similar embeddings is easy to follow.

The method achieves strong results on ASL-DVS (99.80%) with a very small model (0.35 MB) and a small fraction of training data, and near-SOTA on DVS Gesture, demonstrating that heavy event-to-frame preprocessing may be unnecessary for classification.

Training details, hyperparameters, dataset splits (deterministic, non-random to aid reproducibility), and inference-averaging procedures are reported with unusual care, and code/models/logs are stated to be released.
The discussion of sampling strategies (with vs. without replacement, including a collector's-problem analysis motivating the choice) is a practical contribution for handling very long event streams.
weaknesses: Overstated novelty: the claim of the 'first event to vector representation' is not substantiated against prior work that embeds events as tokens for transformer/sequence models, and against ViT-style patchify-and-embed or point-cloud tokenization approaches. The core recipe (look up an embedding per coordinate, add a temporal encoding, feed to a sequence model) is standard; the paper does not clearly delineate what is new beyond the framing.

Key design choices are not ablated. There is no experiment comparing the proposed parametric neighborhood embedding against a standard lookup-table embedding (Eq. 2), no ablation of the bi-directional linear attention extension, and no ablation of temporal encoding vs. sinusoidal/learnable alternatives. Consequently, the accuracy gains cannot be attributed to event2vec rather than to the gated-linear-attention backbone.

The central theoretical claim is essentially vacuous: Eq. (3)-(6) only show that a continuous network yields similar outputs for nearby inputs, which is true of any continuous embedding and says nothing about whether this inductive bias improves learning. No empirical evidence is provided that neighborhood semantics matter.

The claim of processing events 'directly without losing any temporal resolution' (abstract, discussion) is contradicted by the method itself: 8192 events are sampled from streams of up to 1.6M events, discarding most of the temporal information, and inference is stochastic (accuracy averaged over 18 repeats), which undermines both the resolution claim and deployment claims.

Evaluation breadth is thin for an ICML paper: only two small classification datasets, one of which (DVS Gesture) yields sub-optimal accuracy (96.01% vs 97.92%). Standard larger benchmarks (N-Caltech101, CIFAR10-DVS, ImageNet-DVS) and non-classification tasks (detection, optical flow, tracking) where temporal resolution matters are absent.

Table 1 comparisons are weakly controlled: baselines differ in preprocessing, backbone, and training budget, and the 'Used Training Data (%)' metric is nonstandard and inconsistently defined; no variance or confidence intervals are reported despite stochastic training/inference.

Presentation and completeness issues: the code URL in the abstract is empty, there is no limitations section, the abstract/discussion promise follow-up capabilities (event-GPT, multimodal LLMs) that are entirely speculative, and minor errors ('ASL-DLV', duplicate BERT citations [19]/[27]) suggest insufficient polish.

The word2vec motivation is superficial: word2vec embeddings are learned from distributional co-occurrence statistics via a self-supervised objective, whereas event2vec embeddings are produced by a randomly initialized MLP trained only for a downstream classification task; the 'vector' representation is never validated intrinsically (e.g., analogy/neighborhood structure in embedding space).

strengths: The paper is clearly written and the core idea — treating raw AER events as tokens with a learned spatial embedding plus a continuous temporal encoding — is simple and well-motivated; the analogy between words and events in Section 2 is a nice framing device.

The proposed architecture is lightweight (0.35–3.22 MB) and achieves the best reported accuracy on ASL-DVS (99.80%), with hyperparameters, seeds, and sampling procedures described in enough detail to aid reproducibility.
The authors are honest that DVS Gesture performance is sub-optimal relative to prior work, and they fix a deterministic train/test split to ease fair comparison.
weaknesses: The central methodological claim is not supported by ablation. The paper's main contribution is the parametric embedding (Algorithm 1) over the trivial lookup-table embedding (Eq. 2), yet no experiment compares the two, tests the neighborhood-semantics hypothesis (Eq. 3), or isolates the temporal encoding design. The Taylor-series argument (Eqs. 5–6) is trivial — any continuous MLP satisfies it — and is presented as if it were a substantive theoretical contribution.

Novelty is overclaimed. Calling this 'the first event to vector representation' ignores a substantial body of work that tokenizes/embeds raw events for transformers (e.g., point-based and token-based event transformers, event point cloud methods), and the similarity between events and vocabulary tokens has been implicitly exploited in prior tokenized event models. Related work is not seriously differentiated.

Headline claims contradict the method. The paper claims to process events 'directly without losing any temporal resolution,' but inference randomly samples only 8,192 of ~362,000 events (DVS Gesture) or 512 events (ASL-DVS) — a massive, uncontrolled information discard. The latency/temporal-resolution arguments against conversion methods therefore apply to the proposed method as well, in a more severe form.

The evaluation is narrow and the comparisons are not apples-to-apples. Only two small classification datasets are used; the 'Used Training Data (%)' column is a non-standard, ambiguously defined metric that makes efficiency claims hard to verify; baseline accuracies are quoted from prior papers without re-running them under matched conditions; and test accuracy depends on random event sampling (averaged over 16–18 repeats), unlike baselines that use full streams.

The most emphasized benefit — alignment with NLP/LLMs enabling 'event-GPT' and multimodal models — is entirely speculative. No pretraining, generative, or transfer experiment supports it, so the abstract's central selling point is unsupported by evidence.

No limitations discussion is provided; the code/models/training-logs URL is missing from the manuscript ('available at' with no link), weakening the reproducibility claims; and there are multiple signs of insufficient polish: BERT appears twice as references [19] and [27], 'queries and keys' mislabels k[t], v[t] in Eq. 7 (they are keys and values), 'ASL-DLV' typo, and undefined notation in Algorithm 1 (P vs. 2).

The sampling analysis (Section 4.2, invoking the collector's problem) justifies the chosen scheme but does not empirically compare with-replacement vs. without-replacement sampling, leaving the design choices unsubstantiated.

strengths: The core idea is clean and appealing: drawing the analogy between events and tokens (finite index space, contextual meaning) and embedding events directly into a vector space so that standard sequence models can be applied without event-to-frame conversion.

The parametric spatial embedding (Algorithm 1) is a simple, elegant way to inject neighborhood smoothness into the embedding via a continuous coordinate MLP, and it can be implemented either as a generated lookup table or evaluated directly.

Practical efficiency results are notable: on ASL-DVS the model reaches 99.80% with a 0.35 MB model using only ~512 randomly sampled events per stream, and on DVS Gesture it reaches 96.01% while consuming far fewer training passes than frame-based baselines.

Reproducibility is addressed well: seeds fixed, hyperparameters per dataset are fully specified, and code, models, and training logs are stated to be released. The non-random train/test split is disclosed explicitly to aid fair comparison.
The analysis of sampling with vs. without replacement (using the collector's-problem argument) is a thoughtful and honest treatment of an important practical detail.
weaknesses: The claim of being 'the first event to vector representation' is overstated. Tokenizing/embedding raw events or event point clouds for transformers has been explored in prior event-based vision work, and the proposed spatial embedding is essentially a coordinate-conditioned MLP (closely related to NeRF-style positional/coordinate encodings). The paper does not sufficiently position itself against this related line of work, weakening the originality claim.

Evaluation is narrow: only two small classification datasets (DVS Gesture, 11 classes; ASL-DVS, 24 classes) and five baselines. No experiments on standard larger benchmarks (e.g., CIFAR10-DVS, N-Caltech101, ImageNet-DVS, HardVS), and no tasks beyond classification, so the broader claims (edge deployment, ms-level end-to-end latency, multimodal/LLM integration) remain speculative.

On DVS Gesture the method is below the compared baselines (96.01% vs. 97.80-97.92%), which the authors attribute to dataset scale but do not investigate. The headline efficiency metric 'Used Training Data (%)' is nonstandard, conflates epochs with sampling strategy, and makes the comparison table difficult to interpret fairly.

The claim of processing events 'without losing any temporal resolution' is contradicted by the method itself: at inference the model uses only 8192 (DVS Gesture) or 512 (ASL-DVS) randomly sampled events per stream, discarding the vast majority of events (e.g., streams of over 1.5M events). Sampling-based subsampling trades temporal/spatial coverage for efficiency and should be framed as such.

Inference is nondeterministic and the reported accuracy is an average over 16-18 repeated random samplings. This amounts to a form of test-time ensembling; single-pass accuracy and variance/statistical significance are not reported, so the effective performance of a deployed single-shot model is unclear.

No ablation studies are provided. The contributions of the parametric spatial embedding (vs. a plain lookup table), the learned temporal encoding (vs. sinusoidal/relative encodings), and the bidirectional extension of gated linear attention (vs. unidirectional) are not individually validated, so the evidence does not isolate what drives the results.

The theoretical content is thin: the Taylor-series argument for smooth embeddings is straightforward, and notation/typos ('o^n', 'ASL-DLV', incomplete code URL in the abstract, 'p_o' in Fig. 1) reduce polish.

There is no limitations section; the Discussion consists largely of aspirational future directions (event-GPT, multimodal LLMs) rather than an honest accounting of the method's constraints, such as sensitivity to sampling size, applicability to dense prediction, and behavior on longer/harder datasets.
